statement: Opioid agonist maintenance treatment (methadone or buprenorphine) roughly halves all-cause and overdose mortality in people with opioid use disorder versus being out of treatment.
effect_size: ~50% reduction in all-cause and overdose mortality during treatment; highest risk in the weeks after leaving treatment
population: People with opioid use disorder (systematic review/meta-analysis of cohort studies)

provenance.primary: Sordo et al., BMJ 2017 — Mortality risk during and after opioid substitution treatment

confidence_notes: Strongest treatment-mortality finding in addiction medicine. Cohort (not RCT) by ethical necessity but large and consistent. Detox-alone without maintenance is associated with WORSE outcomes (tolerance loss -> overdose).

statement: Addiction involves real, measurable neuroadaptations in reward, motivation, learning/memory, and prefrontal inhibitory circuits across three stages (binge/intoxication, withdrawal/negative affect, preoccupation/anticipation).
effect_size: Qualitative circuit-level model with neuroimaging support
population: Humans and animal models with substance use disorders

provenance.primary: Volkow, Koob & McLellan, NEJM 2016 — Neurobiologic Advances from the Brain Disease Model of Addiction

confidence_notes: The neuroadaptation is real (mechanism). The strong inference 'therefore chronic, choiceless brain disease' is an outcome/framing claim that overreaches the mechanism (honesty rule #1) and conflicts with remission data.

statement: Most people who meet criteria for drug dependence remit, the majority by their early thirties and most without formal treatment, a natural-recovery pattern inconsistent with a purely chronic progressive brain disease.
effect_size: Majority remission among ever-dependent in national surveys; much of it untreated ('maturing out')
population: US national epidemiological surveys (NESARC/NCS) of substance dependence

provenance.primary: Heyman, Addiction: A Disorder of Choice (Harvard University Press, 2009); Robins Vietnam veteran studies (1970s)

confidence_notes: Serious critique, not fringe. Does NOT mean addiction is trivial or pure willpower; means it is responsive to incentives/context. Corpus indexes the disease-vs-choice conflict as open-but-converging (both partly true).

statement: For every common drug, the majority of people who ever use it never transition to dependence; transition probability varies by drug (nicotine highest ~68%, then opioids/alcohol/cocaine ~21-23%, cannabis ~9%).
effect_size: Cumulative probability of dependence among ever-users: nicotine ~68%, cocaine ~21%, alcohol ~22%, cannabis ~9% (order-of-magnitude)
population: ~43,000 US adults, NESARC

provenance.primary: Lopez-Quintero et al., Drug Alcohol Depend 2011 — Probability and predictors of transition from first use to dependence

confidence_notes: Honesty rule #2 in data form: refutes 'one hit and you're hooked.' Relative addiction potential, not precision. Consistent with Anthony/Warner/Kessler 1994.

statement: Physical dependence (tolerance + withdrawal) is normal pharmacological adaptation and is not the same as addiction (compulsive use despite harm); DSM-5 abolished the abuse/dependence split for a single dimensional substance use disorder.
effect_size: Definitional/categorical
population: General (clinical nosology, DSM-5 2013)

provenance.primary: DSM-5 (APA, 2013) reclassification of substance use disorders as a dimensional construct

confidence_notes: High-confidence definitional point. Conflating dependence with addiction underlies the 'replacing one drug with another' anti-MAT canard and the mislabeling of pain patients as addicts.

statement: Varenicline and combination nicotine-replacement therapy are the most effective pharmacological smoking-cessation aids (~2-3x placebo quit rates); cytisine is non-inferior; behavioural support multiplies effect.
effect_size: Varenicline RR ~2.3 vs placebo; combination NRT superior to single-form; cytisine non-inferior to varenicline
population: Adult smokers attempting cessation (network meta-analysis of RCTs)

provenance.primary: Cahill et al., Cochrane 2013 — Pharmacological interventions for smoking cessation: network meta-analysis; Courtney et al., JAMA 2021 (cytisine, DOI 10.1001/jama.2021.7621)

confidence_notes: Varenicline's earlier neuropsychiatric black-box concern was cleared by EAGLES. Cross-ref Section 09 for combustion-vs-nicotine harm and vaping harm-reduction grading.

statement: Naltrexone (reduces heavy drinking) and acamprosate (supports abstinence) have real but modest efficacy for alcohol use disorder (number-needed-to-treat ~12); both are cheap, generic, and under-prescribed.
effect_size: NNT ~12 (acamprosate for return-to-any-drinking; naltrexone for return-to-heavy-drinking)
population: Adults with alcohol use disorder, outpatient (systematic review/meta-analysis of RCTs)

provenance.primary: Jonas et al., JAMA 2014 — Pharmacotherapy for Adults With Alcohol Use Disorders in Outpatient Settings

confidence_notes: Modest but real and comparable to many accepted treatments. The treatment gap is cultural as much as clinical. Disulfiram works only with supervised adherence.

statement: Abrupt cessation in physically dependent heavy alcohol or benzodiazepine users can cause seizures and delirium tremens with real mortality; severe cases require benzodiazepine-supported supervised detox (alcohol) or slow taper (benzodiazepines).
effect_size: Delirium tremens carries meaningful mortality if unmanaged; benzodiazepine withdrawal can cause seizures
population: Physically dependent heavy alcohol / chronic benzodiazepine users

provenance.primary: Established clinical-toxicology consensus (e.g., ASAM alcohol-withdrawal management guidelines)

confidence_notes: Distinguishes alcohol/benzo from opioids: opioid withdrawal is agonizing but rarely directly fatal; alcohol/benzo withdrawal can be. 'Cold turkey' is safe advice for nicotine, dangerous for severe alcohol/benzo dependence.

statement: No pharmacotherapy is robustly effective or FDA-approved for cocaine or methamphetamine use disorder; the best-evidenced treatment is the behavioural intervention contingency management.
effect_size: No medication with consistent benefit for cocaine use disorder; modest signal for bupropion + naltrexone in methamphetamine
population: Adults with cocaine/methamphetamine use disorder (systematic reviews of RCTs)

provenance.primary: Chan et al., J Gen Intern Med 2019 — Pharmacotherapy for Cocaine Use Disorder: a systematic review and meta-analysis

confidence_notes: Honest null on medication. The field's biggest pharmacological hole. Behavioural lever (CM) exists but is under-used.

statement: Contingency management (tangible rewards for verified abstinence) is the most effective psychosocial treatment for stimulant use disorder, with an observed mortality association, yet it is severely under-used because rewarding abstinence offends a moral intuition.
effect_size: Largest effect sizes among psychosocial treatments for stimulants; CM participation associated with lower mortality in cohort data
population: Adults with stimulant use disorder (meta-analyses of RCTs + cohort)

provenance.primary: AJP 2025 — Contingency Management for Stimulant Use Disorder and Association With Mortality (cohort); broad CM meta-analytic literature

confidence_notes: Under-deployment is driven by moralism over evidence. Where pharmacology fails (stimulants), CM is the main lever.

statement: Community overdose education and naloxone distribution (OEND) reduces opioid overdose mortality by putting a fast-acting reversal agent in the hands of people who use drugs and bystanders.
effect_size: Reduced overdose mortality in communities with real, wide distribution
population: People who use opioids and their social networks; syringe-service-program participants

provenance.primary: CDC MMWR 2020 — Overdose Education and Naloxone Distribution Within Syringe Service Programs; multiple program evaluations

confidence_notes: Does not treat addiction; keeps people alive long enough to access treatment. Keystone of harm reduction.

statement: Manualized Twelve-Step Facilitation (clinician-delivered linkage to AA) produces alcohol-abstinence outcomes at least as good as, and often better than, other active treatments and is more cost-effective; the bare advice 'go to meetings' is not the same intervention, and AA's culture fits some people and repels others.
effect_size: TSF >= CBT/other active treatments on continuous abstinence; superior cost-effectiveness
population: Adults with alcohol use disorder (Cochrane review of RCTs)

provenance.primary: Kelly et al., Cochrane 2020 — Alcoholics Anonymous and other 12-step programs for alcohol use disorder

confidence_notes: Strong evidence is for STRUCTURED TSF, not the bare slogan. Real, effective, free, widely available -- but one tool, not the only tool, and not a substitute for MAT in opioid/alcohol use disorder.

statement: Gambling disorder is the only broadly accepted behavioural addiction; DSM-5 reclassified it with substance addictions on the basis of shared phenomenology and reward-circuit biology, and it carries high suicide risk.
effect_size: Shared reward-circuit biology and clinical course with substance addictions; elevated suicide risk
population: Adults with gambling disorder

provenance.primary: Potenza et al., Nat Rev Dis Primers 2019 — Gambling disorder

confidence_notes: The bar the contested behavioural constructs (food/sex/internet/phone) have not cleared. CBT best-evidenced; naltrexone shows a signal; Gamblers Anonymous thinly evidenced.

statement: Food, sex, internet/gaming, and phone/social-media 'addiction' are contested constructs where the addiction label outruns the evidence; the WHO (ICD-11) and APA (DSM-5) openly disagree on gaming and explicitly classify compulsive sexual behaviour as an impulse-control disorder, not an addiction.
effect_size: Real compulsive/harmful patterns in a minority; construct validity and substance-vs-behaviour classification unresolved
population: General population (heterogeneous self-report instruments)

provenance.primary: DSM-5 (gaming = condition for further study; no sex/porn/phone diagnosis) vs ICD-11 (gaming disorder included; compulsive sexual behaviour = impulse-control, not addiction)

confidence_notes: Honesty rule #1: 'addiction' doing rhetorical work the evidence hasn't licensed. Self-labelled 'porn addiction' correlates more with moral disapproval of one's use than with amount of use. Grade the construct, not the vibe.

statement: Cannabis use disorder is real (~9% of ever-users, ~17% with adolescent onset, higher in daily users); adolescent and high-THC exposure is associated with psychosis risk in the vulnerable; chronic use can cause cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome.
effect_size: ~9% lifetime dependence among ever-users (rising to ~17% with adolescent onset); dose-related psychosis association
population: Cannabis users (cohort/epidemiological)

provenance.primary: Volkow et al., NEJM 2014 — Adverse Health Effects of Marijuana Use; Hall, Addiction 2016 (DOI 10.1111/add.13428)

confidence_notes: Not harmless, not the devil. Cannabis-psychosis causation vs shared vulnerability still debated but signal consistent. Today's high-THC product is not the plant of older epidemiology. No approved medication for the disorder.

statement: Classic psychedelics (psilocybin, LSD, mescaline, DMT) have very low addiction potential -- not reliably reinforcing, rapid tolerance discourages bingeing -- with risks that are psychological rather than dependence-related.
effect_size: Negligible dependence/compulsive-use signature
population: Psychedelic users (epidemiological + pharmacological)

provenance.primary: Established pharmacology of 5-HT2A agonist psychedelics; cross-ref Section 20 6.4 for the therapy frontier

confidence_notes: Belong outside the addiction conversation prohibition lumped them into. The psychedelic-assisted-therapy frontier (incl. as treatments FOR addiction) is early/unblindable/not-approved -- graded in Section 20 6.4.

statement: Caffeine produces genuine physical dependence with a recognized withdrawal syndrome, but DSM-5 lists caffeine use disorder only as a condition for further study; for most users it is a benign dependence.
effect_size: Reliable withdrawal (headache, fatigue, low mood) peaking ~1-2 days after cessation; clinically significant addiction uncommon
population: Regular caffeine users

provenance.primary: DSM-5 (caffeine withdrawal/intoxication recognized; use disorder = condition for further study); controlled caffeine-withdrawal trials

confidence_notes: Illustrates honesty rule #2: dependence is common and usually benign, and is not the same as addiction. Taper to quit without withdrawal.

statement: The belief that an addicted person must hit 'rock bottom' before recovery is possible is false; early intervention works, people recover from every severity, and motivational approaches are built on the opposite premise that ambivalence is workable now.
effect_size: Motivational interviewing and early intervention effective without any 'bottom'
population: People with substance use disorders

provenance.primary: Motivational interviewing evidence base (Miller & Rollnick); natural-remission data (Heyman)

confidence_notes: Dangerous myth that rationalizes withholding help and waiting for catastrophe. Refuted by MI efficacy and remission-from-all-depths data.

statement: Anaesthesia-assisted ('ultra-rapid') opioid detox is expensive, medically risky (deaths have occurred), and does nothing for the addiction itself -- detox is not treatment, and by lowering tolerance it can raise overdose risk.
effect_size: No benefit over standard care for sustained recovery; serious adverse events including death
population: People with opioid use disorder

provenance.primary: Clinical evidence on anaesthesia-assisted rapid opioid detoxification; tolerance-loss overdose mechanism (cf. Sordo 2017)

confidence_notes: Detox is not treatment. Compresses withdrawal while leaving craving/cues/context intact; lowered tolerance makes relapse more lethal.

statement: The claim that one-size-fits-all 12-step abstinence is the only legitimate path to recovery is an overclaim; multiple effective paths exist (MAT, CBT, contingency management, motivational interviewing, and for some, moderation rather than abstinence).
effect_size: Several evidence-based treatment paths with comparable or superior outcomes for different people
population: People with substance use disorders

provenance.primary: Composite of MAT (Sordo 2017), pharmacotherapy (Jonas 2014), CM, MI, and TSF (Kelly 2020) evidence bases

confidence_notes: TSF works AND is not universal -- both true. Historic insistence that everyone must do AA and be abstinent forever failed the large minority it didn't fit. Goal should be severity-stratified, not dogmatic.

statement: Syringe service programs reduce HIV/HCV transmission without increasing drug use, and harm-reduction measures (naloxone, drug checking, supervised consumption) keep people alive and connected to care; the abstinence-vs-harm-reduction framing is a false binary.
effect_size: Reduced infectious-disease transmission and overdose death; no increase in drug use ('enabling' worry not supported)
population: People who use drugs accessing harm-reduction services

provenance.primary: Syringe-service-program and OEND evidence base (incl. CDC MMWR 10.15585/mmwr.mm6933a2)

confidence_notes: Controversy is moral/political more than empirical. Abstinence is a fine goal but a deadly precondition for receiving help; harm reduction keeps people alive to reach abstinence if/when they choose it.
